newsitem.title: UK: Exchange rate to play second fiddle at BOE meeting.
newsitem.headline: Exchange rate to play second fiddle at BOE meeting.

text.p: The strength of the pound and the power of the foreign exchanges is likely to be a hot topic at this week's meeting of the Bank of England monetary policy committee.
The views of Bank governor Eddie George and chief economist Mervyn King on the subject are well known.

George acknowledges the strong pound poses a policy dilemma but, scarred by his experience of 1987 when interest rates were cut to try and weaken sterling despite growing domestic demand, he has made it clear the exchange rate will not guide policy.
King roughly agrees. In the May quarterly bulletin, he said while the exchange rate is important the Bank will not subscribe to any target or rule.

"Although the exchange rate is an important component of our assessment of the economy and the prospects for inflation, it is not wise to succumb to the superficial attraction of a 4:1 rule," he wrote.
George and King are likely to find support from one of the two new outside members of the monetary policy committee at this week's meeting.

Indeed, an article in the weighty academic journal "Economic Policy" reveals Willem Buiter, Professor of International Macroeconomics at Cambridge University, views activity on the foreign exchanges and those who trade in them with near disdain.
"It is important not to stand in too much awe of the market," he wrote in the April edition, penned before his appointment.

"Foreign exchange traders and those who provide them with information, from chartists to reconditioned rocket scientists, are not an especially well-informed breed. They are often extremely myopic: the long run is, in many cases, the end of their trading day."
He said the views of foreign exchange dealers change at the drop of a hat, and as individuals they are nervous, jittery and "in need of a good night's rest".
However, he concedes that since they command very large resources, governments ignore them at their peril.
"Governments have to pay attention to them in the same way adults have to pay attention to children armed with Uzis," he concludes.
